problem_plain: Modern AI models spend most of their time waiting for data to travel from memory chips to the processor, not actually doing math. When a model generates a single word, it must haul tens of gigabytes of stored numbers — its learned weights and the model's running notes — across a wire that can only move a fraction of that data per second. The processor sits idle most of the time, starved for numbers to work on.
why_plain: The chips that do math have gotten dramatically faster over decades, but the wires connecting chips to memory have not kept pace — moving a byte still takes roughly the same time it did years ago. This gap between math speed and data-movement speed is called the memory wall, and AI workloads hit it especially hard because they read enormous tables of learned numbers and the model's running notes in patterns that defeat simple tricks for keeping data nearby.
approach_plain: The papers in this theme attack the memory wall from three directions: bringing the math closer to where data already lives (doing math inside the memory), smarter decisions about which data lives where and for how long (tiering, fetching data early, compressing, and smarter eviction), and restructuring how programs hand data between storage layers (computing near or inside the storage drive, using a fast link to extra memory, and tuning hardware and software together). Together they aim to cut the number of bytes that must cross any wire before useful work happens.

groups.heading: Running math inside or right next to memory chips
groups.explain: Instead of shipping data from memory to a processor, these designs place small math units inside or immediately beside the memory chip itself. A memory chip's internal wiring carries far more data per second than any external wire, so doing even simple math there — multiplying rows of numbers by a single column, computing distances, adding things up — can eliminate most of the costly external data movement. This is what 'doing math inside the memory' means.

papers.name: CENT
papers.gloss: Skips the GPU; 32 memory modules with built-in math units give 2.3x more answers at 5.2x lower cost.

papers.name: PAPI
papers.gloss: A live monitor routes each model step to whichever chip fits — math-heavy or data-movement-heavy.
Runs computing-on-locked-data math on in-memory chips by keeping related numbers physically close; 4 to 209 times faster.

papers.name: PUSHtap
papers.gloss: Lets the main CPU and in-memory math units share database rows without format conversion; 3.4x faster queries.

papers.name: AsyncDIMM
papers.gloss: Lets the host chip and a memory module's math unit run simultaneously instead of taking turns; 1.19 to 1.92 times faster.

papers.name: PROCA
papers.gloss: Runs random-guess-and-check sampling inside memory chips; predicts early if a guess will be accepted; up to 4,871 times faster.

papers.name: PAISE
papers.gloss: Moves the step where each new word checks the model's running notes to in-memory math units; up to 48% faster.

papers.name: FACIL
papers.gloss: Lets the in-memory math unit and the main chip read learned weights at once, without copying twice; 2.4 to 2.6 times faster.

papers.name: Piccolo
papers.gloss: Places only a lightweight traffic router inside memory chips, not full math; avoids wasted reads; 3.28x faster.

papers.name: UniNDP
papers.gloss: One software toolkit programs many in-memory chip designs using one common language; 1.05 to 3.43 times better mapping.

papers.name: GoPIM
papers.gloss: Runs graph-learning networks on resistance-based memory chips with a learned resource planner; 191 times faster.

papers.name: EOD
papers.gloss: Combines compressed graph data inside a chip beside memory without decompressing first; 981 times faster on that step.

papers.name: NMP-PaK
papers.gloss: Places pipelined math units inside memory module buffers for genome assembly; bandwidth used rises from 6.5% to 44%.

papers.name: ANSMET
papers.gloss: Math units beside memory compute rough distances and stop reading early when a match is too far away; 8x faster.

papers.name: HeterRAG
papers.gloss: Pairs cheap memory math units for lookup steps with fast memory math units for number-crunching in one retrieve-then-generate system.

papers.name: OptiPIM
papers.gloss: Automatically maps a neural network to an in-memory chip as a math optimization problem, solved in under four minutes; 1.9x better.

papers.name: DReX
papers.gloss: Memory-chip logic filters far-away entries before they leave; a nearby math unit searches what remains; 6 to 7 times faster.

papers.name: ATiM
papers.gloss: A compiler automatically splits and schedules math for a commercial in-memory chip without hand-coding; up to 8.2 times faster.

papers.name: DX100
papers.gloss: Reorders up to 16,384 indirect lookups before sending them to memory; gives 500 times more look-ahead; 2.6 times faster.

papers.name: Stratum
papers.gloss: Stacks in-memory processors above a tall memory chip; predicts which weights are needed next and moves them up; 8.3x faster.

papers.name: Pimba
papers.gloss: Two memory banks share one math unit, interleaving reads with writes to halve chip area; 4.1 times more words per second.

papers.name: ORCHES
papers.gloss: GPU reads the prompt while in-memory units generate words simultaneously, overlapping both steps; 4.2 times speedup.

papers.name: FALA
papers.gloss: Reused data goes through fast on-chip memory; single-use data goes through in-memory math units; 1.56 times faster.

papers.name: Ecco
papers.gloss: A compress-and-expand unit squeezes weights and running notes 4 times between on-chip and off-chip memory; 2.9 times faster.

papers.name: REIS
papers.gloss: Math inside a storage drive's controller finds close matches and fetches documents together, skipping a round-trip to the main chip.
A math unit inside a storage drive converts a text query and searches for close matches entirely inside; 4.3x faster than CPU.

papers.name: CrossBit
papers.gloss: Adds wires inside flash chips so bit operations span multiple columns; enables filtering inside the chip; 2.1 times faster.

papers.name: Folded Banks (FB-HBM)
papers.gloss: Redistributes memory sub-banks across a tall stacked chip via short vertical wires, replacing slow long horizontal ones.

papers.name: MagiCache
papers.gloss: Each fast on-chip memory row dynamically switches between storing data and doing math; chains of instructions hide wait time.

papers.name: MVE
papers.gloss: New math instructions describe four-dimensional access patterns; mobile chip uses 60% of compute lanes instead of 23%; 2.9x faster.

papers.name: ASDR
papers.gloss: Maps 3D scene reconstruction onto in-memory chips; nearby camera rays share data to avoid repeated chip reads.

papers.name: CMSwitch
papers.gloss: First compiler to detect when an in-memory chip can switch its arrays between math mode and storage mode per layer; 1.31x faster.

papers.name: ER-DCIM
papers.gloss: An in-memory chip corrects its own math errors in real time at low voltage using a compact checking code on each operation.

papers.name: HyFlexPIM
papers.gloss: Fine-tuning puts the most important model weights in reliable single-bit cells; the rest use two-bit cells; 1.86x more throughput.
First real-hardware test of a commercial in-memory chip under retrieve-then-generate work; three layout changes give 54 to 118x less energy.

groups.heading: Using a fast link to extra memory: giving a server more memory through a high-speed cable
groups.explain: A fast link to extra memory is a new electrical standard that lets a server treat extra memory modules, storage drives, or even other compute boards as if they were directly attached RAM, plugged into the same slot a graphics card uses. This expands how much memory a server can see without redesigning its processor chip. The catch is that this extra memory arrives 140 to 410 billionths of a second later than memory on the main board, so systems must be smart about what lives in fast memory versus slow memory and when to move data between them.

papers.name: Melody
papers.gloss: Runs 265 programs on four real fast-link memory devices, breaking each access into sub-steps to pinpoint bottlenecks.

papers.name: HybridTier
papers.gloss: Tracks both lifetime-read count and recency of each memory page to place it in fast or slow memory; up to 91% faster.

papers.name: M5
papers.gloss: Puts access counters inside the fast-link controller chip itself at 64-byte granularity; moves only hot bytes; 14% faster.

papers.name: CTXNL
papers.gloss: Lets database code turn off consistency checking per item where it is not needed; 2.1 times the throughput.

papers.name: ByteFS
papers.gloss: Routes small random reads through the byte path and large writes through the block path of a dual-mode storage drive.

papers.name: SkyByte
papers.gloss: A write buffer inside the drive's controller bridges byte reads and page writes; 6 times faster than a plain fast-link drive.

papers.name: LIA
papers.gloss: Offloads large math steps to CPUs with built-in multiplication hardware; a fast link holds more of the model; 19x lower delay.

papers.name: CXLfork
papers.gloss: Copies a running program to a remote server via fast-link shared memory without serializing its full state; 87% less local memory.

papers.name: ArtMem
papers.gloss: A learning agent moves pages between fast and slower extra memory, stopping when the fast tier has room; up to 172% faster.

papers.name: UGPU
papers.gloss: Carves one GPU into unequal sections; uses short vertical wires in a stacked chip to move pages between layers in parallel.

groups.heading: Fetching data early: getting data before the processor asks for it
groups.explain: Fetching data early means a hardware or software unit predicts what data will be needed soon and retrieves it from main memory in advance, hiding the wait time behind ongoing math. These papers design smarter early-fetch systems that handle irregular patterns — following pointers through a graph, doing indirect lookups like 'go to position B[i] and read A there' — that defeat simple approaches which only work when data is read in a straight line.

papers.name: Gaze
papers.gloss: Learns which memory addresses are read together in a region and fetches them early; 5.7 to 11.4% more instructions per second.

papers.name: Alecto
papers.gloss: Picks the best early-fetch strategy for each memory request based on its access type; cuts tracking-storage energy 48%.

papers.name: MOKA/DRIPPER
papers.gloss: Decides per fetch whether crossing a page boundary is worth it, using a learned predictor on address-lookup busyness; up to 3.3% faster.

papers.name: RecMG
papers.gloss: Separate learned models guide fast-memory placement and early fetching for recommendation lookup tables; 43% faster answers.

papers.name: Magellan
papers.gloss: A compiler maps data dependencies across nested loops to handle multi-level indirect lookups; 1.14x faster, 25% fewer stalls.

papers.name: Prophet
papers.gloss: Adds run-time hints into a program's binary to help early-fetch hardware manage bookkeeping storage better; 14% faster.

papers.name: IPEX
papers.gloss: Suppresses early fetches on energy-harvesting devices when data will be lost before the next power outage; saves 7.9% energy.

papers.name: MAMA
papers.gloss: Each CPU core fetches aggressively, but a central supervisor caps total bandwidth to prevent flooding the memory wire; 2.1% more work.

papers.name: TSP+MRS
papers.gloss: Fetches a short task's data the moment it joins the queue; a scheduler holds the task until data arrives; 3.1x faster.

papers.name: Hierarchical Prefetching
papers.gloss: Groups related code into named bundles and fetches a whole bundle when any entry is detected; 6.6% gain over the prior best.

papers.name: Skia
papers.gloss: Keeps a record of recently evicted branch targets so instruction-fetch keeps predicting correctly after the main table fills.
A joint policy stops the address-lookup table and instruction cache from each evicting the same code and then both re-fetching it.

papers.name: EDBP
papers.gloss: Identifies fast on-chip memory slots that won't be read before the next power outage and powers them off early; saves 9.8% energy.

papers.name: SoMa
papers.gloss: Plans data fetches from memory chips across several fused network layers at once rather than per layer; 2.1x faster, 37% less energy.

papers.name: NUPEA
papers.gloss: On chips with many small math units in a grid, places data-load instructions on units nearest the data; 28% faster.

papers.name: CHESS/SBP
papers.gloss: Records the branch-decision path of previous cloud requests and replays it for new similar requests; within 5% of a warm predictor.

papers.name: Phelps
papers.gloss: Runs all hard-to-predict branches in a helper thread each loop; feeds results to the main thread in order so it never stalls.
Shows simple in-order chips can use value guessing without recovery logic; recovers 86% of the speed advantage; 38% more instructions per clock.
Predicts branches early by noticing only one or two outcome combinations occur; cuts early-prediction energy from 14.6x to 1.5x normal.

papers.name: DeepContext
papers.gloss: Links Python code calls to the GPU operations they trigger, showing the real bottleneck; guided fixes give up to 1.66x speedup.

groups.heading: Deciding what to keep and what to throw out of fast on-chip memory
groups.explain: Fast on-chip memory holds only a small amount of data. When it fills up and new data arrives, something must be thrown out. Choosing badly means the processor has to re-fetch that data from slow memory chips very soon. These papers design smarter eviction rules — often by watching past access patterns, using hints from the compiler that wrote the program, or managing both instruction and data streams together in chips with many cores.

papers.name: Garibaldi
papers.gloss: Protects data from eviction when the instruction that loaded it will need it again soon; 13.2% faster, 10% less energy.

papers.name: TRRIP
papers.gloss: Compiler labels code blocks hot, warm, or cold; fast memory keeps hot blocks at top priority; 3.9% faster, 27% fewer instruction misses.

papers.name: IBM Telum Cache
papers.gloss: IBM's Telum II spreads fast memory across stacked chips with an adaptive hold-time rule; keeps 90%+ of processors busy on mixed workloads.

papers.name: PACIPV
papers.gloss: Tests every insertion and promotion rule combination to find the best fast-memory policy for servers; matches learned policies cheaply.

papers.name: FLACK/FURBYS
papers.gloss: Derives the theoretical best eviction rule for the decoded-instruction store; a practical version cuts misses 14% and improves performance per watt 3.1%.

papers.name: Drishti
papers.gloss: Trains a reuse predictor across all fast-memory slices but keeps samples local per slice; nearly doubles prior eviction gains on 32 cores.

papers.name: Avalanche
papers.gloss: Reorders matrix columns for skipping-unimportant-numbers math so related data lands in the same fast-memory slot; 1.97x faster.

papers.name: Gemina
papers.gloss: Merging identical pages and grouping small pages into large ones together preserves 96% of memory savings with 43% less lookup-speed loss.

papers.name: OASIS
papers.gloss: Detects stable versus shifting data access patterns across a many-GPU system; assigns different copy policies per phase; 64% faster.

papers.name: Necro-reaper
papers.gloss: New instructions let the compiler tell hardware to skip saving data already freed; cuts data movement 26%, raises throughput 6%.

papers.name: TDRAM
papers.gloss: Adds comparison circuits inside a tall stacked chip so the chip itself checks whether it holds a requested address; 1.23x faster.

papers.name: MPW
papers.gloss: Groups GPU address-translation requests that share page-table structure and sends multiple in parallel; cuts queue wait 87%, raises throughput 56%.

papers.name: Heliostat
papers.gloss: Reuses GPU 3D-rendering address-traversal hardware as extra address-translation engines; 1.93x faster at 1.5% of the chip area.

papers.name: NACHO
papers.gloss: Builds write-after-read tracking into the fast on-chip memory controller for energy-harvesting devices; 54% less runtime overhead.

papers.name: WarmCache
papers.gloss: Magnetic-resistive fast memory with a relaxed hold time survives short power outages; compiler fixes drifted bits on restart; 1.3 to 1.4x faster.

papers.name: Pivot
papers.gloss: Prioritizes only memory requests from important tasks that are actively blocking the processor pipeline; 2.76x more background work done.

papers.name: IRIS
papers.gloss: A camera chip reuses edge and motion maps to score region importance; shrinks low-importance regions before saving; 55% less bandwidth.

groups.heading: Managing the model's running notes for fast AI serving
groups.explain: Large language models keep a record of the conversation so far — the model's running notes — that grows with every new word and can fill the GPU's memory entirely. These papers focus on moving, compressing, or scheduling these running notes so they do not become the bottleneck when many users are asking questions at the same time.

papers.name: Aqua
papers.gloss: Moves the model's running notes to a neighboring GPU when a request is paused, not to slow CPU memory; 4x more answers.

papers.name: NEO
papers.gloss: Reads the model's running notes on the CPU while the GPU reads learned weights simultaneously; up to 7.5x more throughput.

papers.name: FPDT
papers.gloss: Trains on 2 million-word sequences by streaming chunks; GPU processes one while the next travels across the chip-to-chip wire; 16x longer.

papers.name: LLM.265
papers.gloss: Reuses the GPU's built-in video encoder and decoder as a compressor for weights, intermediate values, and running notes without new silicon.

papers.name: GSArch
papers.gloss: Labels 3D-scene data units hot or cold; keeps hot units in fast on-chip memory during training; up to 6.5x faster.
Exact document-match search beats approximate search end-to-end because fewer but more relevant results give the model less to read.

groups.heading: Computing near or inside the storage drive: filtering data before it leaves the drive
groups.explain: Storage drives hold far more data than any memory chip, but reading data from a drive and sending it to the processor wastes bandwidth on items that will be thrown away immediately. These papers push simple computation — filtering rows, matching names, compressing, finding close matches — into the storage device itself so only the relevant fraction of data ever travels across the wire.

papers.name: UPP
papers.gloss: Compiles any database filter into a compact instruction set that runs on stored data inside a flash drive; 1.2 to 7.9x faster.

papers.name: ANVIL
papers.gloss: Matches name keys inside flash chips of a standard solid-state drive; only matches leave the drive; 4 to 25x faster.

papers.name: Fusion
papers.gloss: Lays out files so filter rules run at storage nodes before data crosses the network, cutting data transferred for selective queries.

papers.name: FEDORA
papers.gloss: Stores a privacy lookup table on solid-state drives instead of memory chips; extends drive lifetime 158x and cuts round-trip delay 24x.

papers.name: CCZNS
papers.gloss: Restores hardware compression inside sequential-write-only drives by compressing internally and telling the host where each chunk ends.

papers.name: OS2G
papers.gloss: A smart network card reads training data from cloud storage and drops it directly into GPU memory, bypassing the main CPU entirely.
Data loading is 88 to 91% of graph-learning training time; reading directly from a solid-state drive into GPU memory is 15x faster.

papers.name: YOUMU
papers.gloss: Reads training data from a compressed column-format file using random page access, skipping format conversion; 80% less memory per node.

papers.name: AnyKey
papers.gloss: Redesigns key tracking for a key-value drive so metadata stays bounded in size regardless of key length, separating identity from content.

papers.name: ZRAID
papers.gloss: Stores incomplete safety-backup calculations in the drive's own write buffer rather than a reserved zone, removing the throughput bottleneck.

papers.name: Zebra
papers.gloss: Uses a sequential-write drive's random-write buffer to absorb incomplete safety-backup updates in a drive array; 1.1 to 4.2x faster.

papers.name: RpcNIC
papers.gloss: A smart network card batches writes and keeps serialized data in host memory to avoid slow cross-bus transfers; 2.3x faster processing.

groups.heading: Memory reliability, system management, and infrastructure
groups.explain: As systems push memory chips harder — more rapid row reads per second, lower voltages, denser storage — physical reliability becomes a concern. Reading one row of a memory chip repeatedly at high speed can secretly flip bits in the neighboring rows — an attack on memory reliability that existing defenses try to prevent but have not fully solved. Separately, cloud systems need smarter rules for placing workloads and keeping tenants isolated. These papers study these challenges and propose fixes.

papers.gloss: Tests 160 chips and finds the repeated-read bit-flip threshold varies 3.5x across measurements on the same chip, undermining every existing defense.

papers.name: ColumnDisturb
papers.gloss: Reading one row disturbs up to 3,072 neighboring rows via shared column wires, far more than the classic bit-flip attack.

papers.name: PuDHammer
papers.gloss: Doing math inside a memory chip activates multiple rows, lowering the bit-flip threshold up to 158x versus the classic attack; first measurement.

papers.name: Pegasus
papers.gloss: Maps failing memory addresses to the virtual machines whose data lives there; only at-risk machines are moved; 70%+ less migration cost.

papers.name: FleetIO
papers.gloss: One learning agent per cloud customer manages shared solid-state drive resources; agents learn together to balance isolation against utilization.

papers.name: Tela
papers.gloss: Models how storage server load changes over time and places virtual disks to stay balanced across predicted future periods.

papers.name: Virtuoso
papers.gloss: Simulates virtual memory management by imitating observed operating-system decisions, enabling fast chip-plus-OS co-design without a full OS.
Simplifies flash management on tiny microcontrollers by merging separate steps into coarser logic, cutting wasted writes without a wear-balancing layer.

papers.name: Ariadne
papers.gloss: Mobile swap uses fast-expanding chunks for relaunch data and compact chunks for cold data; starts expanding before the user switches; 50% faster.

papers.name: Stramash
papers.gloss: Runs one operating system kernel across two chips with different instruction sets, using shared memory as the link; 2.1 times faster.

papers.name: Wave
papers.gloss: Moves operating-system housekeeping to a smart network card's processors, freeing 16 main CPU cores with only 1.1 to 7.4% slowdown.

papers.name: Concord
papers.gloss: Multiple nodes hold a readable data copy and discard it when a write happens; 2.4 times faster and 1.7 times more throughput.

papers.name: InfiniMind
papers.gloss: A brain-implant memory controller learns from neural signals on a non-volatile chip; four write-reduction methods extend chip lifetime 23x.
Predicts smart-network-card task speed under shared load, accounting for CPU time, data movement, and queue space competition.

papers.name: Gigaflow
papers.gloss: A virtual network switch caches intermediate processing stages on a smart card, not just full lookups, staying fast with large rule sets.

papers.name: BTrace
papers.gloss: Redesigns a smartphone event-recording buffer to never drop events, even at slightly lower peak speed, to reliably capture crashes.

papers.name: BYOM
papers.gloss: Each app trains a small model to score storage jobs for fast versus spinning drives; placements use live capacity feedback.

papers.name: I-DGNN
papers.gloss: Rewrites a time-evolving graph-learning network as one chain of multiplications, removing repeated passes per graph update; 65 to 71% faster.

papers.name: MeHyper
papers.gloss: A chip for data where one link connects many nodes computes each shared intermediate value only once; 1,032x faster than CPU.

groups.heading: Restructuring data layouts and how bandwidth is used for specific workloads
groups.explain: Memory chips deliver data in fixed chunks of 64 bytes at a time, but many workloads — graph analytics, genome assembly, math with mostly-zero entries, satellite imaging — only need a few bytes from each chunk. These papers restructure data layouts, computation order, or hardware so most of each fetched chunk is actually used, directly raising how much useful work gets done per byte moved without making the memory chips any faster.

papers.name: NOVA
papers.gloss: Separates gather-neighbors and send-updates steps so the full graph stays in memory without being re-read multiple times; 2.35x faster.

papers.name: Chason
papers.gloss: An FPGA chip for mostly-zero matrix multiplication moves non-zero values across channels to balance use; 8x faster than prior FPGA designs.

papers.name: SPARK
papers.gloss: Converts 1.4% of a CPU's fastest on-chip memory into a helper that skips zero-multiplications; 15x faster than a desktop CPU.

papers.name: Buffalo
papers.gloss: Spreads high-connection graph node data across non-adjacent memory sections so billion-node graph training does not overflow GPU memory; 71% faster.

papers.name: GSplit
papers.gloss: Assigns graph nodes to GPUs via a probability map so each GPU handles a non-overlapping set; no redundant loading; 4.4x faster training.

papers.name: pulse
papers.gloss: Runs pointer-chasing code at the memory module where the data lives, removing repeated round-trip delays across a rack-scale network.

papers.name: StreamGrid
papers.gloss: Processes 3D point clouds in a grid-by-grid streaming way with fixed on-chip memory; 10x faster, 3.9x better energy than prior chips.

papers.name: ARC
papers.gloss: Combines multiple GPU threads' update writes into one before reaching the update handler, reducing conflicts during 3D rendering training.

papers.name: OctoCache
papers.gloss: Reorders 3D map traversal so nearby nodes are accessed together and parallelizes independent updates; 45 to 88% faster map construction.

papers.name: GPUlog
papers.gloss: Runs a rule-based logic query language on a GPU using a structure combining index updates with dense array operations; 45x faster.

papers.name: Earth+
papers.gloss: Compresses satellite images on board by sending only changed pixels versus a nearby satellite's reference image; 3.3x less data sent.

papers.name: SEAL
papers.gloss: A chip inside an image sensor encodes brightness as time delay and tracks features before data leaves; 16 to 61x less delay.

connect: Every paper in this theme — whether it moves math into memory, fetches data early, compresses numbers, or filters results at the storage drive — is solving the same physical problem: the wires that carry data between chips are slower and costlier per bit than the math units that process it, so the only way to make AI systems faster is to move less data, not do less math.
